analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 41, Lavender Ladner, Petitioner v. United States of America. Mr. Rosenwald. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. In this case, there was an indictment in three counts under Section 254 of former Title 18 of the United States of Code. The first count charged the petitioner with conspiring with another person named Cameron to violate Section 254 by conspiring by means of deadly and dangerous weapons to assault two agents of the alcohol tax unit of the Treasury Department. The second count alleged that at the same time and place the petitioner and Cameron actually did assault one such agent named Reed and assaulted him by the use of a deadly and dangerous weapon to wit a loaded shotgun. The third count charged a similar assault with a loaded shotgun against a second alcohol tax unit agent named Fox. The second count stated that the federal agent who was the victim of the assault was seriously wounded. The third count simply alleged that the federal agent there involved was wounded. The defendant, the petitioner rather, was arraigned, placed on trial in the District Court in Mississippi, and pleaded not guilty. He was found guilty by the jury on all the three counts. And on the same day, he was sentenced to two years on the first count to be concurrent with the sentence on the second count, to ten years on the second count, to ten years on the third count, and the ten years on the third count, the sentences under the second and third count to be consecutive, are a total of twenty years. There was no transcript of the evidence at the trial whatsoever. There was no appeal taken from the conviction at that time. There is nothing of evidence in this record before the court. There is, it crept into the record some way, and after David, taken before a federal investigative agent, which I don't know whether it was in evidence in the trial, it shouldn't have been, and it was rejected by the Court of Appeals as having any value or bearing on this case. After serving more than ten years, the petitioner filed a motion under Section 2254 of Title 28 to correct his sentence. This motion was filed on January 22, 1955. The motion alleged that the sentences under the, that the offenses charged in the second and third counts were only a single offense, and therefore the sentences under those two counts should not have been consecutive. The motion doesn't clearly state, but it surely implies, that at the time of the offense, a gun was used, but was only fired once. And apparently, it is claimed that the, this was a shotgun with pellets scattered, and the one shot struck the two federal agents. The motion of the petitioner was denied by District Judge Myers. On the grounds, stressed that he had a personal recollection that more than one shot was fired, although the trial had occurred more than ten years prior to that time. He admitted there was no transcript taken, and he said that, in any event, each count of the indictment alleged a separate offense, meaning the second and third count alleged separate offenses because separate victims of the shot were named. He also made a statement that the motion had been denied on a prior occasion, and cited as his authority for that statement, his own decision over ruling such a motion filed by the petitioner's co-defendant. And it's quite clear that the petitioner himself had never filed a motion before. The Court of Appeals, for the fifth second, heard the appeal. It was filed by the petitioner. He proceeded in the form of papers in the Court of Appeals. And the Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment of the District Judge, rejected the recollection of the District Judge as having any bearing on the question, found no evidence in the record worthy of consideration by the Court that there was more than one shot fired, and treated the case on the basis that the motion of the petitioner clearly stated that one shot and one shot alone was fired, and that that one shot resulted in the wounding of these two federal agents. And the Court of Appeals held that the one shot, striking the two men, constituted two offenses under Section 254. And the Court, in this Court, granted sessiwere, and the case is here. And we submit, on that narrow question, whether a single shot of a shotgun that strikes two men can constitute more than one offense under Section 254. The government has stated the question quite differently, and we are in complete disagreement with the statement of the question as it's presented. and as it presented, the government's statement is that the shots were fired on the same day and that two federal agents were wounded on the same day or some such language and ignores the critical question in the case, which is whether the single discharge of a shotgun can constitute more than one violation of this statute. Well, Mr. Justice Hawley, I think it may make a difference. If he has a repeating gun or a machine gun that requires only a single impulse, as Mr. Justice Franker used to praise in a recent case, then it might well be that that would only constitute one offense. But clearly, this is the strongest case we can have. There is only one shot. And I would prefer to think of the case on that narrow ground. I stand corrected, Mr. Justice Whitaker. One discharge of the shotgun. And the number of bullets, pellets, or whatever is in a cartridge or using a shotgun, scatter and struck two people. Now, in this case, unlike the two preceding cases, we have no delicate problems of state and federal relations. Nor do we have, as I see the matter, any constitutional questions. We're at home here for the simple matter of construing a statute of the United States Congress. The statute has two clauses. The first clause makes it an offense to forcibly resist, oppose, impede, intimidate, or interfere with certain designated federal officials referred to in the prior section of the code. The second clause of the statute is a statute. The second clause of the statute prescribes the use of a deadly or dangerous weapon in the commission of any of the six forbidden acts mentioned in the first clause of the statute. And prescribes a 10-year penalty for violation where the dangerous weapon is used for nearly three years under the first clause. Now, I think we can almost dispose of this case on the face of the statute itself without going beyond it or any extraneous assistance. The government argues, and the two courts below seem to hold, that this case, that this statute condemned an assault with a dangerous weapon. They completely ignored the other things forbidden by the statute. Now, we have to test the decisions of the court below. Against the statute as a whole. Against the statute as a whole. Resistance, opposing, impeding. Supposed that a person forcefully holds a door against six federal agents who are attempting to enter a room in the performance of their duties. Would this court side? Or would the court below have said, under those circumstances, that there were six separate violations of the statute? Or suppose that instead of using the simple force of his arm, the petitioner the act had waived a club or the butt of a gun, a deadly or dangerous weapon. Or make it a knife, as long as it's deadly and dangerous. And he died. He didn't point it at anybody. He didn't point it at anybody. But he certainly resisted and opposed the weapon. And perhaps added a few threats. The petitioner the act had waved a club or the butt of a gun, a deadly or dangerous weapon. And he died. He didn't point it at anybody. He didn't assault or strike anybody with this weapon. But he certainly resisted and opposed and opposed and perhaps added a few threats. And in such a case if there were ten agents. and perhaps added a few threats. And in such a case, if there were ten agents, would there be ten violations of the statute? Would the man be properly sentenced for ten years to each agent who is affected by his unlawful act? Perfectly willing to agree that he would have violated the statute for how many times? Once to reach an agent affected by what he did. Now, in this case, on the face of the statute, when the petitioner held his shotgun, and before he fired, he violated the statute. He committed an assault. He pointed at them. I assume they knew it was happening, but in any event, he pointed it at them. He made ready to fire. And his offense, they submit was completed then and then. He violated the statute. What happened to those folks? If they hit two federal agents and six, or if they hadn't hit any of them, he violated the statute. But I don't think he violated it more than once. Because the statute says he's agreed to crime to use as dangerous or deadly weapons. And he used it. And that, in my case, it seems to me clear from the face of the statute itself is the unit of prosecution in this case. The use of the gun in whatever way may have been used. The consequences are not material. But the statute seems to imply a distributive use of the various suppositions that you made. And whoever and the commissioners any of the acts describe. Therefore, different acts may have different consequences or be committed in a different context. The statute... The statute... That's true. The statute permits the offense to be committed. even without doing anything that does any harm. I mean... But if he takes your club and hits successively, two agents down the head, in your view, is that one act or two? In my view, that's clearly two acts. Whether it's two offenses depends on another question, which isn't raised in the same question Mr. Dr. Pound. Is this really one transaction or two transactions? We don't have to decide that. It's only one act. I gather from your argument that since mass consequences of a single impulse or act only constitutes the commission of only one offense as to some aspects of the various conducts prescribed by this statute. Therefore, the face of the statute indicates that a single such impulse can mean only one single offense. Isn't that the tenor of your argument? That's the tenor of my argument. One, the face of the statute. In other words, the consequences or the effects or results of what the petitioner did has no bearing on the measurement of his crime. The crime was completed when he did the act, which is forbidden. And that was the use of the deadly weapon. And once he did that, we don't follow the bullets through the air to find what they struck, if anything, because it's not material. He violated the statute, and that's the end of it, once he did that act. Since there was, as I say, only one single act. But the, uh, there is perhaps raised also in this case, a question that's been before this court several times in the last couple of years, of the construction of a statute which is not clear. And for this purpose, I am willing to assume, for the sake of argument, that the government's position, the position of the courts below, is correct. This statute simply says, whoever assaults with a dangerous weapon, and, uh, we will assume that, uh, here you may take into account the consequences, or at least notice that two people were right. Uh, in such cases, similar cases, this court has stated several times that whether or not multiple punishments are intended for the, or to be imposed, or may be imposed, are the consequences of a single criminal act. depends upon the intention of the Congress in adopting the statute. Uh, and in determining that intention, uh, we look at such helplessly find, or may find, in the legislative history of the statute. Uh, the logic, the logical problem is too difficult. It leads us too frequently to an impasse. And, uh, whether one blow constitutes two or more offenses under the common law, whether one shot that strikes two people is one murder or two murders, uh, which is a matter that's been the subject of philosophical consideration by the courts and by text writers. And, uh, it leads into a, uh, great, uh, quagmire of logical difficulties and blind distinctions. That this court is aborted completely in such cases as Bell against the United States, the Prince against the United States, and the CIT credit corporation case. And it's held that this is really a question of what Congress intended. And, uh, we look, define that intention, and if there is no clearly stated intention to impose multiple punishment for a single criminal act, then we resolve the doubts in favor of the criminal defendant. Now, uh, we have examined in our brief the legislative history of Section 254. It's, uh, interesting, but not very illuminating. The statute was introduced at the request of the Department of Justice as, and, uh, in 1934. There was a letter that the Attorney General uh, to Bell, Chairman of the House and Senate Committees and the Judiciary respectively, which was set forth, a letter set forth in full in my brief. And in that letter, the Attorney General requested that the Congress adopt general legislation to protect federal agents, uh, and, uh, he cited specific statutes already in existence, one of which made it an offense to wound the federal laws. Uh, from this, we argue, uh, that, uh, the Congress had before it, uh, a suggestion, at least, or at least it was called to their attention that they might make it an offense to wound a federal officer, and thereby the consequences of the act condemned would be more significant than they are here. But, uh, nevertheless, that, uh, course wasn't followed. There's nothing in the statute about wounding, uh, the statute reads simply as it reads. Uh, at, there's very little more, the debates in, in the Congress are not very helpful. Uh, there was a committee report referred to my brief that does nothing more than paraphrase the statute as it was fondly written, and, uh, I think the, uh, legislative history is frankly helpful, but I can't, uh, say that it overwhelmingly posed that Congress had any specific intention in the matter before the court. No, of course, in these, uh, cases when statutes of this kind are under consideration by the Congress, nobody really, uh, says, well, I'll suppose if somebody shoots a shotgun and hits two people with the same shot, we just have no such specific help, uh, in this case, and just, uh, the faint suggestion that, uh, there was no intention, at least, to, uh, deal with the consequences of the condemned act. Now, but, in the Prince case, there was probably more help for legislative history, but the rule is stated in both Prince and Bell, is that unless the legislative history, as I read those cases, unless the legislative history shows an intention to impose multiple punishments, the court will not impute that intention to Congress, because these penalties are too high, and, uh, I decided the number of cases where multiple punishments were imposed in my brief could show just how harsh they can be, they can be terrific. I did refer in the brief to the legislative history of section 111 of, uh, under the 1948 revision of the criminal statutes, title 18, section 254 involved in this case, and section 118 of former title 18 were combined to form this new section, one of 11, of title 18, which covers the ground at the peasant time. And, uh, this section 118 that was combined with 254 is traced back to the criminal code of 1909 and to the original enactment of that statute in 1905. That statute was a more specific statute of the of Animal Industry of the Department of Agriculture. And in its original version, that statute provided that it was an offense to discharge any deadly weapon at any officer or employee of the Bureau of Animal Industry, or to use a deadly or dangerous weapon in resisting it. And the offense was clearly defined in that statute as discharging any weapon. In other words, offense was done when the weapon was discharged, that was, and the consequences were not material. I submit that that statute, oh, pardon me, those words about discharging a deadly weapon were dropped when the statute was included in the 1909 criminal code. And I suggest in my brief that the reason for the omission is that the words were considered redundant. They were really covered by the words, the use of a deadly or dangerous weapon. that the two-statute section 250, no, that we can therefore infer that it was understood by Congress in adopting the criminal code of 1909 that the statute meant what it had originally said, that it's the use of the weapon or the discharge of the weapon that was condemned, that the consequences were not material, you didn't look to them. I've been discouraged by the statements of this court in the Prince case and in the Bell case, not to refer to cases decided under other statutes, and yet it seems that this is all is gone, so I will mention just a few of them. The leading one, I think, is the Bell case, in which this court held that the transportation of two women at the same time in interstate commerce in the same vehicle, and on the same occasion for immoral purposes constituted only one violation of the man act, that we don't count the number of victims of the unlawful conduct, that the deed is single and the offense is single.
